::: {.callout-note}
## About these data
The Zambia and Bangladesh newborn screening data are **openly available** on
Dryad ([doi:10.5061/dryad.m37pvmd6b](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.m37pvmd6b)).
The reference GA is from a first-trimester dating ultrasound. The Ontario
development data cannot be shared, but the **fitted Ontario models** are used
here exactly as they were for the published external validations. Minor
differences from published numbers are expected because missing analytes are
handled more simply here: batch-mean imputation instead of multiple imputation.
:::

# Setup

```{r setup}
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "forcats", "ggplot2", "glmnet", "glmnetUtils"))
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnetUtils)
library(splines)

source("code/ga_functions.R")   # original pipeline (prep.data, pareto_log, ...)
source("code/gavars.R")         # original derived variables (af_ratio, SGA, ...)
source("code/ga_preprocess.R")  # frozen preprocessing (section 4)
source("R/metrics.R")           # AUC with DeLong CI, etc.
source("R/plots.R")             # theme and palette
source("R/real_data.R")         # loading and scoring helpers

options(width = 200)
pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)

full_model <- readRDS("code/full_model_pto_relax.rds")  # Ontario: clinical + analytes
bw_model   <- readRDS("code/bw_model_pto_relax.rds")    # Ontario: birthweight, sex, multiple
cohorts    <- load_all_cohorts("data")
```

# Meet the data

## Four cohorts, two countries, two sample types

```{r cohort-table}
bind_rows(cohorts) |>
  group_by(Cohort = cohort) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            `Preterm (<37 wk)` = sprintf("%d (%s)", sum(preterm01), pct(mean(preterm01))),
            `<34 wk` = sum(gestage < 34),
            `SGA (<10th)` = pct(mean(sga10 == 1)),
            `Median birthweight (g)` = median(bweight_raw),
            Multiples = sum(multiple == "multiple"),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(match(Cohort, COHORTS$cohort))
```

Preterm infants are **rare** in every cohort: 11 in Zambia heel samples, 35
in Bangladesh heel samples. Keep that in mind when you see the confidence
intervals below.

## Birthweight for gestational age differs between the two countries

```{r bw-ga, fig.height=4.2}
heel <- bind_rows(cohorts[c("Bangladesh heel", "Zambia heel")])
ggplot(heel, aes(gestage, bweight_raw, colour = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL_COUNTRY) +
  labs(x = "Reference GA (weeks)", y = "Birthweight (g)",
       title = "Bangladeshi infants are lighter at every gestational age",
       subtitle = "Heel-prick cohorts; lines are loess smoothers") +
  theme_seminar()
```

About 1 in 4 Bangladeshi infants is small for gestational age, against about
1 in 12 in Zambia. A model that leans on birthweight will
**underestimate GA** wherever growth restriction is common.

## Which analytes track gestational age?

```{r correlations, fig.height=5.5}
num_vars <- c("bweight_raw", "af_ratio", LOG_VARS)
cors <- bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  data.frame(cohort = k, variable = num_vars,
             rho = sapply(num_vars, function(v)
               cor(d[[v]], d$gestage, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")))
}))
top <- cors |> group_by(variable) |> summarise(m = mean(abs(rho))) |>
  slice_max(m, n = 15) |> pull(variable)
cors |>
  filter(variable %in% top) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = rev(top)),
         variable = forcats::fct_recode(variable, Birthweight = "bweight_raw",
                                        `Adult/fetal Hb ratio` = "af_ratio"),
         country = sub(" .*", "", cohort), sample = sub(".* ", "", cohort)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rho, variable, colour = country, shape = sample)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = INK2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL_COUNTRY) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(heel = 16, cord = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Spearman correlation with reference GA", y = NULL,
       title = "Haemoglobin ratio and birthweight carry most of the signal") +
  theme_seminar()
```

Only the adult/fetal haemoglobin ratio and birthweight correlate with GA
beyond |ρ| ≈ 0.3. The rest of the model's accuracy comes from combining many
weak signals, which is why it uses penalised regression.

## Heel and cord blood are different samples

The same infants often gave both a heel-prick and a cord-blood sample, so we
can compare the two directly:

```{r heel-cord, fig.height=4.5}
pairs_bd <- inner_join(
  cohorts[["Bangladesh heel"]] |> select(pair_id, gestage, N_17OHP, TSH, TYR, af_ratio),
  cohorts[["Bangladesh cord"]] |> select(pair_id, N_17OHP, TSH, TYR, af_ratio),
  by = "pair_id", suffix = c("_heel", "_cord"))
pairs_long <- bind_rows(lapply(c("N_17OHP", "TSH", "TYR", "af_ratio"), function(v)
  data.frame(analyte = v, heel = pairs_bd[[paste0(v, "_heel")]],
             cord = pairs_bd[[paste0(v, "_cord")]])))
pairs_long |>
  filter(heel > 0, cord > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(heel, cord)) +
  geom_abline(colour = INK2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1, colour = COL_COUNTRY[["Bangladesh"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ analyte, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Heel prick", y = "Cord blood",
       title = sprintf("Same %d Bangladeshi infants, two sample types", nrow(pairs_bd)),
       subtitle = "Dashed line = equal values (log scales)") +
  theme_seminar()
```

17-OHP is about five times higher in cord blood, while TSH and tyrosine are
lower. A model trained on heel-prick samples sees cord blood as a
**shifted population**, even for the very same infant.

## Laboratory and population differences between countries

```{r hb, fig.height=3.8}
heel |>
  select(country, `Raw HbF (% of peak)` = HGB_F, `Adult/fetal Hb ratio` = af_ratio) |>
  pivot_longer(-country) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Raw HbF (% of peak)", "Adult/fetal Hb ratio"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = country)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = COL_COUNTRY) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density",
       title = "Raw HbF differs between the countries; the ratio barely does") +
  theme_seminar()
```

A **ratio** of two measurements from the same run cancels much of the
between-laboratory calibration difference. Feature choices affect
transportability.

## Data quality

```{r missing}
bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  data.frame(cohort = k, variable = c("af_ratio", LOG_VARS),
             missing = sapply(c("af_ratio", LOG_VARS), function(v) mean(is.na(d[[v]]))))
})) |>
  filter(missing > 0.05) |>
  mutate(missing = pct(missing)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cohort, values_from = missing, values_fill = "<5%")

sapply(cohorts, function(d) sum(d$TSH <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))   # non-positive TSH values
```

Zambia has substantial missingness for several analytes, and some TSH values
are ≤ 0 (below the detection limit). External data are rarely as clean as the
development data.

# External validation of the Ontario model

Both Ontario models are applied exactly as in the published validations.
Each cohort is standardised on itself before scoring (see section 4).

```{r score}
for (k in names(cohorts)) {
  cohorts[[k]]$pred_full <- score_site_standardised(cohorts[[k]], full_model, alpha = 0.75)
  cohorts[[k]]$pred_bw   <- score_site_standardised(cohorts[[k]], bw_model)
}
```

## Accuracy, with bootstrap confidence intervals

```{r perf}
perf_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  bind_rows(lapply(c(`Clinical + analytes` = "pred_full",
                     `Birthweight, sex, multiple` = "pred_bw"), function(v) {
    b <- boot_perf(d$gestage, d[[v]], B = 1000)
    g <- function(m) b[b$metric == m, ]
    data.frame(
      Cohort = k, n = nrow(d),
      `MAE (wk)` = with(g("MAE"), fmt_ci(estimate, lower, upper)),
      `Within 7 days` = with(g("within_7d"), fmt_ci(estimate, lower, upper, d = 0, pct = TRUE)),
      `Bias (wk)` = with(g("bias"), fmt_ci(estimate, lower, upper)),
      `MAE preterm` = with(g("MAE_preterm"), fmt_ci(estimate, lower, upper)),
      check.names = FALSE)
  }), .id = "Model")
}))
perf_tab |> relocate(Cohort, Model)
```

* Heel-prick MAE is about 0.8 weeks in both countries, close to the 0.7 weeks
  in the Ontario test set. Cord blood is worse.
* The confidence intervals for **preterm infants** are wide: 11–35 preterm
  infants per heel cohort is not enough to pin down subgroup accuracy.

## Calibration and regression to the mean

```{r cal-real, fig.height=6.5}
all_scored <- bind_rows(cohorts) |>
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = COHORTS$cohort))
ggplot(all_scored, aes(pred_full, gestage)) +
  geom_abline(colour = INK2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = country), alpha = 0.3, size = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = INK, linewidth = 0.9,
              formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ cohort, nrow = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL_COUNTRY) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(27, 43), ylim = c(27, 43)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted GA (weeks)", y = "Reference GA (weeks)",
       title = "Reference vs predicted GA, Ontario full model") +
  theme_seminar()
```

```{r rtm-real, fig.height=4.2}
plot_regression_to_mean(rename(cohorts[["Bangladesh cord"]], ga_ref = gestage),
                        pred = "pred_full") +
  labs(title = "Bangladesh cord: errors against reference vs predicted GA")
```

This is the same pattern as in the simulation: infants **born** preterm are
predicted too old (left), because of regression to the mean.

## Where the analytes earn their keep: small-for-gestational-age infants

```{r sga}
bind_rows(cohorts) |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(sga10 == 1, "SGA (<10th centile)", "Not SGA")) |>
  group_by(Cohort = cohort, group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            `Bias, birthweight model` = mean(pred_bw - gestage),
            `Bias, full model` = mean(pred_full - gestage),
            `MAE, birthweight model` = mean(abs(pred_bw - gestage)),
            `MAE, full model` = mean(abs(pred_full - gestage)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  arrange(match(Cohort, COHORTS$cohort), desc(group))
```

The birthweight model reads growth restriction as immaturity: it
underestimates GA in SGA infants by 1.5–3.3 weeks. The metabolic profile
largely corrects this. That matters most in settings where SGA is common.

## Heel vs cord in the same infants

```{r paired-perf}
paired_perf <- function(country) {
  h <- cohorts[[paste(country, "heel")]]; c <- cohorts[[paste(country, "cord")]]
  j <- inner_join(select(h, pair_id, gestage, heel = pred_full),
                  select(c, pair_id, cord = pred_full), by = "pair_id")
  data.frame(Country = country, `Paired infants` = nrow(j),
             `MAE heel` = mean(abs(j$heel - j$gestage)),
             `MAE cord` = mean(abs(j$cord - j$gestage)),
             `Within 7 d, heel` = pct(mean(abs(j$heel - j$gestage) <= 1)),
             `Within 7 d, cord` = pct(mean(abs(j$cord - j$gestage) <= 1)),
             check.names = FALSE)
}
bind_rows(paired_perf("Bangladesh"), paired_perf("Zambia")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Same infants, same reference GA: the difference is due to the **sample type**
alone. That is a measurement shift, not a population shift.

## Discrimination for preterm birth

Predicted GA itself is the score: the lower the predicted GA, the more likely
preterm.

```{r auc-real}
bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  a3 <- auc_ci(d$preterm01, -d$pred_full); a1 <- auc_ci(d$preterm01, -d$pred_bw)
  data.frame(Cohort = k, `Preterm infants` = sum(d$preterm01),
             `AUC, full model` = fmt_ci(a3[1], a3[2], a3[3], 3),
             `AUC, birthweight model` = fmt_ci(a1[1], a1[2], a1[3], 3),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
```

AUCs are high for the full model everywhere. With so few preterm infants,
though, the estimates are imprecise: the birthweight model's interval in Zambia
heel samples runs from about 0.64 to 0.99, and asymptotic intervals such as
DeLong's are themselves unreliable with 11 events. Current guidance for
external validation studies is to plan sample size around the **number of
events** (often 100 or more) and the precision needed for calibration as well
as discrimination (Riley et al., *BMJ* 2024).

## Counting preterm births: a surveillance use case

```{r prevalence}
bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  data.frame(Cohort = k, `Observed preterm` = pct(mean(d$preterm01)),
             `Predicted GA < 37 wk` = pct(mean(d$pred_full < 37)),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
```

Counting infants whose **predicted** GA is below 37 weeks underestimates the
preterm birth rate, sometimes by half. This is regression to the mean again:
predictions are pulled toward term. For population surveillance, estimate the
rate by averaging calibrated predicted probabilities, not by counting
classifications.

# Does a prediction depend on the batch it is scored in?

The published pipeline standardises each dataset **on itself** before scoring
(`prep.data()`), and the model's spline knots are written as
`knots = quantile(x, ...)`, which is re-evaluated on whatever data are being
scored. So an infant's prediction can depend on **who else is in the batch**.

## The same infants, scored in different batches

```{r batch, fig.height=4.2}
bh <- cohorts[["Bangladesh heel"]]
set.seed(11); idx_random <- sample(nrow(bh), 60)
set.seed(12); idx_enriched <- c(sample(which(bh$preterm01 == 1), 30),
                                sample(which(bh$preterm01 == 0), 30))
batch_df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(batch = "Random batch of 60",
             full_cohort = bh$pred_full[idx_random],
             own_batch = score_site_standardised(bh[idx_random, ], full_model, 0.75)),
  data.frame(batch = "Batch of 60, half preterm",
             full_cohort = bh$pred_full[idx_enriched],
             own_batch = score_site_standardised(bh[idx_enriched, ], full_model, 0.75)))
batch_df |>
  group_by(batch) |>
  summarise(`Mean shift (wk)` = mean(own_batch - full_cohort),
            `Mean |change| (wk)` = mean(abs(own_batch - full_cohort)),
            `Largest |change| (wk)` = max(abs(own_batch - full_cohort))) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))

ggplot(batch_df, aes(full_cohort, own_batch)) +
  geom_abline(colour = INK2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(colour = COL_COUNTRY[["Bangladesh"]], alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ batch) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Predicted GA, scored within the full cohort",
       y = "Predicted GA, scored as its own batch",
       title = "Same infants, same model, different answers") +
  theme_seminar()
```

In a batch that is half preterm, standardisation re-centres the batch, and
every prediction is pulled **toward term**. A single infant cannot be scored at
all. The published cohort-level results are not wrong, but the validated
"model" includes a site-level re-standardisation step. That step:

* can absorb laboratory calibration differences (helpful);
* assumes the new population's GA and birthweight mix resembles Ontario's
  (risky where preterm birth or SGA is common);
* needs a representative batch, so it cannot score infants one at a time.

## The fix: learn every constant once, in the reference data

`code/ga_preprocess.R` stores the floor, winsorisation cap, centre, scale and
spline knots from the reference data, and applies them unchanged. Until the
Ontario constants are available, the **Bangladesh heel cohort stands in as the
reference** to demonstrate the mechanics:

```{r frozen}
ref_raw <- cohorts[["Bangladesh heel"]]
prep_ref <- ga_prep_fit(ref_raw, LOG_VARS, NOLOG_VARS,
                        reference_label = "Bangladesh heel (stand-in)")
set.seed(1); ref_pto <- prep.data(ref_raw)
fit_rows <- complete.cases(ref_pto[, c(LOG_VARS, NOLOG_VARS)])
knots_ref <- ga_knots_fit(ref_pto[fit_rows, ], SPLINE_VARS, type = "bs_range")
bundle_ref <- ga_bundle(ga_freeze_terms(full_model, knots_ref), prep_ref,
                        knots_ref, alpha = 0.75)
check_batch_invariance(bundle_ref, cohorts[["Zambia heel"]], n = 40)
```

The frozen constants also give a **covariate-shift table**: how far each
variable in a new cohort is from the reference, in reference SD units. Look
at it before looking at outcomes.

```{r shift}
shift_top <- function(target, label) {
  ga_shift(ga_prep_apply(cohorts[[target]], prep_ref)) |>
    head(6) |>
    transmute(Comparison = label, variable,
              `SMD vs reference` = round(smd_vs_reference, 2),
              `% outside reference range` = pct(pct_below_ref + pct_above_ref))
}
bind_rows(shift_top("Zambia heel", "Zambia heel (other site)"),
          shift_top("Bangladesh cord", "Bangladesh cord (other sample type)"))
```

```{r ontario-frozen, eval = file.exists("code/full_model_frozen_bundle.rds")}
# Runs once the Ontario constants have been released from ICES
ont_bundle <- readRDS("code/full_model_frozen_bundle.rds")
bind_rows(lapply(names(cohorts), function(k) {
  d <- cohorts[[k]]
  p <- predict_ga(ont_bundle, d, impute = "reference_mean")
  data.frame(Cohort = k,
             `MAE, site-standardised` = mean(abs(d$pred_full - d$gestage)),
             `MAE, Ontario-frozen` = mean(abs(p - d$gestage)),
             `Bias, site-standardised` = mean(d$pred_full - d$gestage),
             `Bias, Ontario-frozen` = mean(p - d$gestage), check.names = FALSE)
})) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

# What we would do differently next time

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lessons from this case study
1. **The model is the whole pipeline.** Learn every preprocessing constant
   in the training data only, store it with the coefficients, and test that
   predictions do not depend on the batch.
2. **Store spline knots as numbers**, and prefer restricted (natural) cubic
   splines, which are linear beyond the outer knots, for models that will
   travel. B-splines extrapolate as unconstrained cubics.
3. **Look at covariate shift before outcomes**: sample type, laboratory,
   population.
4. **If you standardise per site, do it on purpose.** Describe it as part of
   the model and test its sensitivity to batch composition.
5. **Plan external validation sample sizes around events**, not
   participants.
6. **Justify class-imbalance weights**, and report calibration.
7. **Report the model as coded**, following TRIPOD+AI.
:::
